title: the Gayatri in context
hook: earth, sky, heaven: an Upanishad counts the syllables and finds the Gayatri's first line

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context, and the frame said before the verse: Om, then bhur, bhuvah, svah, earth, the space between, the sky.

A teacher in an old Sanskrit text is playing a counting game. Bhumir, antariksham, dyauh. Earth, sky, heaven. Count the syllables, the text says: eight. The Gayatri's first line has eight too. So whoever knows that first line, it says, wins whatever there is in the three worlds. It sounds like a riddle. It's the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, taking the verse apart line by line. Today: the Gayatri in an Upanishad.
screen: `EARTH, SKY, HEAVEN.` → `COUNT THE SYLLABLES: EIGHT.` → `THE FIRST LINE HAS EIGHT TOO.`

segments.voice: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad gives a whole section to the Gayatri, line by line. The first line is matched by earth, sky and heaven: eight syllables, the three worlds. The second by the three kinds of Vedic verse, the rik, the yajus and the saman: eight syllables, the whole of sacred speech. The third by the three breaths, prana, apana and vyana, the breath in, the breath out and the breath that moves through the body: eight syllables, the whole of life. Worlds, words, breath. Then the text says the Gayatri has a fourth foot. It calls it the visible one, beyond all dust: the sun that blazes. Some readers put it this way: the three lines can be said, and the fourth can only be seen. Then the Upanishad explains the name. In paraphrase: the Gayatri protects the gayas, and the gayas are the breaths; because it protects the breaths, it's called gayatri. That's the Upanishad's own reading of the word, offered as a meditation more than a dictionary entry. It's a big claim made plainly. This one short verse, in the Upanishad's eyes, holds the worlds, the scriptures and the breath of life, and points past itself to a light beyond the dust. The verse we've placed in its hymn and its practice now sits inside the whole of things.
screen: `EARTH, SKY, HEAVEN: EIGHT SYLLABLES.` · `WORLDS, WORDS, BREATH.` · `A FOURTH FOOT: THE SUN THAT BLAZES.` · `IT GUARDS THE BREATHS, SAYS THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Follow one breath all the way in, one all the way out, then notice the breath moving through the body, the small motion in chest and belly, and keep cycling slowly: in, out, through. Every so often, between breaths, leave a gap and notice whatever light there is, on your eyelids, in the room, at the window, without naming it. If you pray, hold the Gayatri's meaning as you go.

The Gayatri in context. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, its three lines hold the worlds, the Vedas and the breaths, and a fourth foot is the blazing sun. It protects the breaths, the text says. Today's word.
Your line: the Gayatri in context. Worlds, words and breath, in three short lines. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use the Upanishads' readings of the Gayatri as a guide for meditation, contemplating the worlds, the Vedas and the breath while reciting or holding the verse.

fork.setup: you've matched three lines to the worlds, the Vedas and the breaths. the Upanishad keeps going. what does it add?

a warning never to recite it
fork.reveal: a fourth foot, the visible one, beyond all dust: the sun that blazes.

original.note: Sanskrit: breath, life-breath; in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad the Gayatri is said to protect the breaths.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gayatri is three lines and that's all.
what it means: the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad reads each line as holding a whole world, and names a fourth foot beyond them.
what a scholar hears: Brihadaranyaka 5.14 calls the fourth foot darshatam padam paro-rajas, the visible foot beyond the dust, and explains gayatri as the one that protects the gayas, the breaths.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

chat.says: Why does that Upanishad say the Gayatri has a fourth foot?
options: It names the visible one beyond the dust, the blazing sun, past the three lines.
It means a fourth line of eight syllables that was lost from the Rig Veda.
It means the verse should be said four times, once for each of the worlds.
chat.meaning: Brihadaranyaka 5.14 calls the fourth foot the visible one beyond the dust, the sun that blazes, past the lines of worlds, words and breath.
